title: Akhand Path, Langar and Nam Japna
content_html:
The Akhand Path

The akhand path is one of the most distinctive and demanding practices in Sikhism. It is the continuous, unbroken reading of the entire Guru Granth Sahib from beginning to end — all 1,430 pages. This takes approximately 48 hours. The reading is divided between a series of readers who take turns, with no gaps in the recitation. At no point is the reading paused or interrupted; when one reader finishes their section, the next begins immediately, even in the middle of the night.

The akhand path is performed to mark significant occasions — festivals such as Vaisakhi and Gurpurbs, major lifecycle events such as the naming ceremony of a new baby or a marriage, occasions of national or community significance, or times of grief. For many Sikh families, beginning a major life event with an akhand path is a way of placing the whole event under the guidance of the eternal Guru. The reading is typically concluded so that the final words are read at a specific time — for a wedding, for example, it ends just before the ceremony begins.

Key Fact

The akhand path is the continuous, unbroken reading of the entire Guru Granth Sahib, taking approximately 48 hours. It is performed at festivals, major life events and times of community significance, placing the occasion under the living Guru’s guidance.

Langar: The Free Communal Kitchen

Langar is the free communal kitchen and meal served at every gurdwara. The word can refer both to the kitchen itself and to the meal it provides. Every person who enters a gurdwara is welcome to eat at the langar, free of charge, with no questions asked. There is no distinction based on religion, caste, ethnicity, social class or gender.

The institution of langar was established by Guru Nanak and developed through the ten Gurus. Guru Amar Das (the third Guru) made it mandatory for visitors to eat in the langar before seeking an audience with him — including, famously, the Mughal Emperor Akbar, who sat on the floor and ate simple vegetarian food alongside everyone else. This was a deliberate, public act of equality.

Langar is understood as an expression of sewa. Preparing and serving the food is tan sewa (physical service); donating ingredients or money to fund the langar is dhan sewa (material service). All volunteers who work in the langar — chopping vegetables, cooking, washing dishes, serving meals — are performing worship. At the Golden Temple (Harimandir Sahib) in Amritsar, the langar serves over 100,000 meals every day, operated entirely by volunteers. At the Gurdwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha in Southall, thousands of meals are served every week.

The langar is traditionally served as vegetarian food so that people of every faith can eat together. Since religious dietary restrictions vary widely — Muslims require halal meat; Jews require kosher food; Hindus may not eat beef; many Buddhists are vegetarian — vegetarian food allows the langar to be truly open to all. This is a practical expression of the Sikh teaching that all people are equal and all are welcome. The Rehat Maryada (the Sikh code of conduct, formalised in 1945) confirms that the langar should be vegetarian. Some amritdhari Sikhs also abstain from meat entirely as a personal spiritual discipline, though this is not a universal Sikh requirement.

Nam Japna: Meditating on the Name of God

Nam japna (also written nam simran) is the practice of meditating on or repeating the name of God. The word nam means “name” (of God) and japna means “to recite” or “to meditate on.” It is one of the three pillars of Sikh teaching alongside honest work (kirat karni) and sharing with others (vand chakna).

Nam japna is practised both individually and communally. In the gurdwara, it takes the form of kirtan — devotional singing of hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib, led by musicians (ragis) playing traditional instruments including the harmonium and tabla. The congregation listens and joins in. Kirtan is understood as a communal form of nam japna — the entire sangat meditating on God’s name through music.

In daily life, nam japna takes the form of the Nitnem — the daily prayers observed by amritdhari Sikhs, beginning with the recitation of Japji Sahib (composed by Guru Nanak) in the early morning. Many Sikh families begin the day by listening to or reciting the Japji Sahib before sunrise. The name most commonly used in nam japna is Waheguru (Wondrous Lord), which may be repeated silently or aloud, alone or in a group, at any time of day.

Guru Nanak taught that the most direct path to mukti (liberation) is through sincere, constant remembrance of God’s name. The Guru Granth Sahib teaches that the mind that turns away from God becomes restless, distracted and vulnerable to the five vices. But the mind that continually returns to Waheguru through nam japna gradually stills the ego (haumai) and opens itself to God’s grace. In this sense, nam japna is not merely a ritual but the fundamental orientation of the gurmukh’s life — the spiritual thread that runs through all other practices, from sewa in the langar to sitting in the sangat during kirtan.

Key Fact

Nam japna is the most direct path to mukti in Guru Nanak’s teaching. Repeating or meditating on Waheguru — in the morning Nitnem, during kirtan, or silently throughout the day — stills the ego, opens the soul to God’s grace, and directly counteracts haumai (self-centredness).

title: Festivals, Birth and Naming Ceremonies
content_html:
Festivals in Sikh Life

Sikh festivals are called melas (gatherings or fairs) and Gurpurbs (Guru anniversaries). Together they mark the cycle of the Sikh year and connect the community to its history, scripture and values. For Sikhs in Britain, festivals are celebrated both at local gurdwaras and, for some families, through visits to India and historically significant gurdwaras.

Vaisakhi (Baisakhi)

Vaisakhi (also spelled Baisakhi) is celebrated in April and is one of the most important festivals in the Sikh calendar. Its religious significance is paramount: it was at Vaisakhi in 1699 that Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa, calling five men from different castes to offer their lives for their faith and initiating them into the first Khalsa brotherhood. This moment is seen as the birth of the Khalsa and a defining moment in Sikh history.

In Britain, Vaisakhi is celebrated with akhand paths in the days leading up to the festival, processions (nagar kirtan) through city streets, kirtan in the gurdwara, langar, and in recent years large public celebrations in cities including Southall, Birmingham and Glasgow. The nagar kirtan is led by the Panj Pyare (five initiated Sikhs who symbolise the original Five Beloved Ones), carrying the Guru Granth Sahib through the streets. It is both a religious celebration and a proud expression of Sikh identity in British public life.

In Punjab, Vaisakhi also coincides with the spring harvest, making it a time of double celebration — the land’s abundance reflecting God’s provision. British Sikhs with family in Punjab often feel a strong cultural connection to the harvest dimension of the festival.

Key Fact

Vaisakhi 1699 was the most significant day in the history of the Sikh community after Guru Nanak’s founding revelation — Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa, created the Panj Pyare, and established the tradition of Amrit Sanskar initiation. In Britain, the nagar kirtan procession on Vaisakhi is one of the largest Sikh public celebrations in Europe.

Divali: Bandi Chhor Divas

Sikhs celebrate Divali but for a specifically Sikh reason: it is called Bandi Chhor Divas — “the day of liberation.” The sixth Guru, Guru Hargobind, was imprisoned in Gwalior Fort by the Mughal Emperor Jahangir. When the Emperor finally agreed to release him, Guru Hargobind refused to leave unless 52 Hindu princes who were also imprisoned were freed at the same time. The Emperor agreed, and Guru Hargobind returned to Amritsar to cheering crowds holding lights — hence the festival of lights.

The story of Bandi Chhor Divas is characteristic of Sikh values: standing for the freedom of others, not just one’s own. Guru Hargobind’s refusal to be freed without the other prisoners reflects the Sikh commitment to justice and equality. It is also significant that the Golden Temple at Amritsar was illuminated to welcome Guru Hargobind back, establishing a tradition of lighting the gurdwara at Divali that continues to this day.

Sikhs and Hindus both celebrate Divali but for different reasons. For many Hindus, Divali marks the return of Lord Rama from exile and the victory of good over evil. For Sikhs, Divali is Bandi Chhor Divas — the release of Guru Hargobind and the 52 princes. This is an important distinction to make in exam answers. The two traditions share the outward customs of lights and fireworks but the religious meanings are distinct. Students should not assume that because Sikhs celebrate Divali they are celebrating the same event as Hindus — Sikhism is a distinct religion with its own historical memory.

A common misconception is to conflate the Naam Karan ceremony with Amrit Sanskar (the Khalsa initiation ceremony). They are distinct. Naam Karan is performed shortly after birth: the baby is brought to the gurdwara, the Guru Granth Sahib is opened at random, and the first letter of the left-hand page determines the child’s name. No vows are taken and no commitment to the Khalsa is made — the ceremony is an act of thanksgiving and of placing the child under the guidance of the Guru’s word from the very beginning of life. Amrit Sanskar, by contrast, is a fully voluntary initiation taken in adulthood (or late adolescence), in which a person chooses to become an amritdhari Sikh and accepts the discipline of the Khalsa Rehat Maryada (code of conduct). A Sikh who has been through Naam Karan has not thereby become an amritdhari — full initiation requires a separate, conscious commitment. Examiners reward this distinction.

Gurpurbs

Gurpurbs are festivals marking anniversaries associated with the Sikh Gurus. The most widely celebrated is Guru Nanak’s birthday (Guru Nanak Gurpurb), usually in November. It is celebrated with an akhand path, kirtan, langar and nagar kirtan. Other major Gurpurbs include the birthday of Guru Gobind Singh and the martyrdom anniversaries of Guru Arjan Dev and Guru Tegh Bahadur (who were executed for refusing to convert to Islam — martyred for the right of religious freedom).

In India, Gurpurbs are celebrated with massive processions, especially in Punjab and at Nanded (where Guru Gobind Singh died). In Britain, Gurpurbs are celebrated in ways that reflect the British context: nagar kirtan through city streets, open days at gurdwaras welcoming non-Sikh visitors, and community events. The way Gurpurbs are celebrated in Britain reflects the diasporic Sikh community’s dual identity — rooted in Punjabi heritage and simultaneously British citizens making their traditions visible in British public life.

Birth and Naming Ceremonies

When a Sikh child is born, thanksgiving to God is expressed at the gurdwara as soon as the mother is well enough. An akhand path may be performed to mark the birth. The formal naming ceremony is called Naam Karan. The family brings the baby to the gurdwara, where the ardas (Sikh prayer of supplication) is offered. The Guru Granth Sahib is then opened at a random page and the first letter of the first hymn on the left-hand page is read aloud by the granthi. The family chooses a name beginning with that letter. This practice expresses the belief that the child’s identity is shaped from the first moment by the Guru’s word.

After the name is announced, the congregation calls out Waheguru Ji Ka Khalsa, Waheguru Ji Ki Fateh (“The Khalsa belongs to the Wondrous Lord; victory belongs to the Wondrous Lord”) as a communal blessing. Karah prashad (a sweet sanctified food made from equal measures of flour, butter and sugar) is distributed to the congregation — the equal portions expressing the equality of all present.

Historic Gurdwaras: The Golden Temple

The Golden Temple (Harimandir Sahib — “Temple of God”) at Amritsar in Punjab is the most sacred site in Sikhism. It was built under the fifth Guru, Guru Arjan Dev, and completed in 1604. Unlike Hindu temples, the Golden Temple was built with four doors, one on each side, signifying that it is open to people from all four directions — a physical expression of the Sikh teaching that all are welcome regardless of caste, religion or background.

The Golden Temple sits in the middle of a sacred pool of water (Amrit Sarovar — the “pool of nectar,” which gives Amritsar its name). Visiting the Golden Temple is considered an act of great devotion. Many British Sikhs make a pilgrimage to Amritsar at some point in their lives, especially at Vaisakhi. Unusually for the Sikh tradition — which does not have an obligatory pilgrimage — visiting the Golden Temple carries deep emotional and spiritual significance for Sikhs worldwide.

Key Fact

The Golden Temple (Harimandir Sahib) at Amritsar was built with four doors — one on each side — to signal that it is open to all people from every direction and every background. This architectural feature is a physical expression of the Sikh belief in the equality of all humanity before God.

title: Sewa and the Sangat
content_html:
What is Sewa?

Sewa is one of the most distinctive and central practices in Sikhism. It is often translated simply as “service” or “volunteering,” but this translation misses the depth of its meaning. In Sikh teaching, sewa is not charity or philanthropy in the secular sense. It is a form of worship — an act of devotion to God expressed through serving God’s creation. To serve another person is to serve the divine light (jot) that is present in them.

This is why the misconception “sewa is just helping others” costs marks in the exam. The Guru Granth Sahib teaches that serving humanity and serving God are not separate acts. A Sikh who prepares food in the langar, or who cleans the shoes of gurdwara visitors, or who donates money to support others, is not merely doing a good deed — they are worshipping God. Sewa is, therefore, inseparable from the Sikh understanding of what it means to be God-centred (gurmukh).

Key Fact

Sewa is understood in Sikh teaching as worship, not merely as charity. Serving another person is serving the divine light present within them. This theological grounding is what distinguishes sewa from secular volunteering and is essential for top-band exam answers.

Three Types of Sewa

Sikh teaching identifies three forms of sewa, each requiring a different dimension of the self:

Tan (physical sewa) is service using the body — cleaning the gurdwara, preparing and serving food in the langar, carrying out building work, or caring for the elderly and sick. At every gurdwara in Britain, including the Gurdwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha in Southall, tan sewa is visible in the hundreds of volunteers who keep the building clean, cook the meals and welcome visitors each week.

Man (mental sewa) is service using the mind — teaching, counselling, offering guidance, providing emotional support, or sharing skills and knowledge with others. Man sewa requires the offering of one’s intellectual and emotional capacities. A Sikh who teaches Punjabi to children at the gurdwara, or who visits isolated elderly members of the community, is performing man sewa.

Dhan (material sewa) is service using material resources — donating money, food or goods to support others. Dhan sewa is understood as an expression of contentment (santokh) and non-attachment to material goods. Sikhs are encouraged to give a daswandh — a tenth of their income — in service, though this is a traditional expectation rather than a legal obligation.

Sewa is not only an outward act of service; it is also a spiritual discipline that fights the greatest barrier to mukti: haumai (ego). When a Sikh volunteers to clean the shoes of gurdwara visitors — a task that in the wider society might be considered beneath one’s status — they are actively dismantling the ego. The very act of selfless service without expectation of recognition or reward trains the mind away from self-centredness and towards God-centredness. In this way, sewa simultaneously serves others and transforms the self. Amritdhari and sahajdhari Sikhs both practise sewa, though amritdhari Sikhs are initiated members of the Khalsa with a deeper formal commitment to sewa as a dimension of their vows.

The Sangat: Religious Community

The sangat is the Sikh congregation or religious community. Guru Nanak placed enormous importance on the company of like-minded believers. In Sikh teaching, the sangat is not simply a social group but a spiritually transforming community — being in the presence of others who are sincere in their devotion to God helps an individual deepen their own faith and resist the pull of the five vices.

The Guru Granth Sahib describes the sangat using the image of iron sharpening iron: just as iron is sharpened by contact with iron, the soul is strengthened and refined by contact with God-centred (gurmukh) people. This is why attending the gurdwara and participating in the sangat is an important part of Sikh life, and why Sikh communities have historically gathered around the gurdwara as their social and spiritual centre.

For Harbhajan, a 15-year-old Sikh in Birmingham, the sangat at his local gurdwara is not just a place of worship — it is where he learns Punjabi, where his family shares meals after Sunday worship in the langar, and where he volunteers each month in tan sewa (cleaning the kitchen and serving food). The sangat provides a community in which faith is lived, not just believed. During times of difficulty — bereavement, illness, hardship — the sangat supports its members practically and emotionally. This holistic, mutual support is understood as an expression of Sikh teaching on the equality and interdependence of all people.

Key Fact

Sewa (particularly tan sewa — physical service such as cleaning the gurdwara) actively counters haumai (ego). Performing humble, self-effacing service without expectation of recognition trains the mind away from self-centredness and towards God-centredness. This is why sewa is understood as both worship and spiritual discipline.

title: Human Life, Sikh Virtues and Mukti
content_html:
The Purpose of Human Life

Sikh teaching holds that human life is an extraordinary gift — the highest form of life in the cycle of rebirth and the greatest opportunity to unite with God. The Guru Granth Sahib describes the human birth as a rare chance: after countless lifetimes in other forms, a soul has been given the capacity to reflect, to choose, and to draw close to Waheguru. This gives human life profound moral weight. Every thought, word and action matters because they affect the soul’s journey.

The goal of human life in Sikh teaching is not simply to live virtuously for its own sake — it is to remove the barriers between the self and God and ultimately to achieve mukti. Mukti is the Sikh understanding of spiritual liberation: the soul released from the endless cycle of birth and rebirth, united with God in a state of joy and peace.

Karma and Rebirth

Sikh teaching includes belief in karma and rebirth. This is a common misconception trap: karma in Sikhism is NOT fate or destiny imposed from outside. It is the natural consequence of a person’s actions. Intentional good deeds, compassion, honest living and devotion to God produce positive consequences; selfish, dishonest or harmful actions produce negative ones. These consequences accumulate across lifetimes.

Crucially, Sikh teaching does not leave a person trapped by karma from previous lives. Through God’s grace (nadar or kirpa) and sincere devotion, even the weight of past karma can be overcome. Guru Nanak taught that God is Gur Prasad — known through grace — and that no soul is so burdened by past actions that it cannot be liberated. This emphasis on divine grace distinguishes Sikh teaching from a purely mechanical view of karma as destiny.

Key Fact

Karma in Sikhism is moral causation, not fate. Good actions, honest living and devotion to God generate positive consequences across lifetimes. But God’s grace (nadar) can transform even a soul burdened by past actions — liberation (mukti) is open to all.

The Five Khands: Stages of Liberation

The Guru Granth Sahib describes the soul’s spiritual journey in terms of five khands (stages or realms). These are not physical places but stages of spiritual development:

1. Dharam Khand (the realm of righteousness) — the stage of moral awareness and righteous living, where souls understand that their actions have consequences and they begin to live according to God’s will. 2. Gyan Khand (the realm of knowledge) — a deeper understanding of God’s creation and the vastness of the divine; the soul gains spiritual wisdom. 3. Saram Khand (the realm of effort) — the soul works hard in spiritual effort, reshaping itself through discipline and devotion. 4. Karam Khand (the realm of grace) — God’s grace begins to operate; the soul is no longer striving alone but is transformed by divine blessing. 5. Sach Khand (the realm of truth) — the final stage, union with God; the soul dwells in the presence of the eternal Truth. This is mukti.

Mukti has both a positive and a negative dimension. Positively, mukti is the joyful merging of the soul with God — described in the Guru Granth Sahib as a state of endless peace, bliss and divine love. The soul is no longer separate from God but lives within the divine presence. Negatively, mukti means release from the cycle of birth and rebirth (samsara) and freedom from the suffering and limitation that physical existence brings. Both dimensions together describe the Sikh understanding of the highest good.

Barriers to Mukti

The Guru Granth Sahib identifies key barriers that prevent a soul from reaching mukti. The greatest is haumai — ego or self-centredness. Haumai is the belief that the self is separate from God and self-sufficient. All other barriers flow from haumai: illusion (maya), lust (kam), anger (krodh), greed (lobh), worldly attachment (moh) and pride (ahankar). These are sometimes described as the five vices (panj dosh). They pull the soul towards the world and away from God.

Sikh teaching describes two fundamental ways of living. A gurmukh (literally “one whose face is towards the Guru”) is a person whose life is oriented towards God. They practise nam simran (remembrance of God’s name), live virtuously, serve others through sewa, and resist haumai. A manmukh (literally “one whose face is towards the mind/self”) lives according to their own ego. They are driven by the five vices and remain trapped in samsara. The aim of Sikh spiritual practice is to move from manmukh to gurmukh.

Sikh Virtues

The Guru Granth Sahib identifies a set of virtues that characterise a gurmukh and support the soul on its journey to mukti. These include: wisdom (the ability to discern God’s will); truthful living (sat — living in alignment with truth and God’s order); justice (treating all people fairly as equally valued by God); temperance and self-control (resisting the pull of the five vices); patience (trusting God’s timing rather than being driven by desire); courage (standing for righteousness, as exemplified by the Sikh martyrs); humility (recognising one’s dependence on God and the worth of others); and contentment (santokh — not being driven by greed or envy).

For Jaspreet, a young Sikh at a gurdwara in Southall, these virtues are not abstract ideals. They are practised through daily nam simran (meditation on God’s name), participation in langar (the free communal meal), and the support of the sangat (religious community). The virtues are worked out in real, everyday life — in how she treats colleagues, how she responds to hardship, and how she serves those around her.

Key Fact

The central barrier to mukti is haumai (ego or self-centredness). The five vices — lust, anger, greed, worldly attachment and pride — all flow from haumai. Cultivating the Sikh virtues — especially humility and contentment — directly counteracts haumai and moves the soul towards liberation.

title: The Gurdwara: Worship and Community
content_html:
What is a Gurdwara?

The word gurdwara means “doorway to the Guru” (from Punjabi: gur = Guru, dwara = door or gateway). Every gurdwara is defined by the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib — the eternal, living scripture that Sikhs regard as their eleventh and final Guru. Without the Guru Granth Sahib, a building is not a gurdwara. This understanding shapes everything about how the gurdwara is designed and used.

There are over 250 registered gurdwaras in the United Kingdom, serving the approximately 430,000 Sikhs in Britain. The largest is the Gurdwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha in Southall, west London — the largest gurdwara outside India — which can accommodate over 3,000 worshippers and serves langar to thousands of people each week. Gurdwaras in cities including Birmingham, Leicester, Bradford and Glasgow are centres of spiritual, cultural and social life for their local Sikh communities.

Design and Features

From the outside, a gurdwara is identifiable by the Nishan Sahib — a tall flagpole flying a triangular dark blue flag bearing the Khanda (the Sikh emblem). Inside, the main prayer hall is called the Darbar Sahib (literally “court of the Lord”). Worshippers remove their shoes and cover their heads before entering as a mark of respect. They then bow before the Guru Granth Sahib and make an offering.

The prayer hall has no fixed seating or pews. The congregation sits on the floor — regardless of age, gender or status — which itself expresses the Sikh belief in equality. There is no distinction between where men and women sit in the prayer hall of a gurdwara; they may sit on either side or intermixed, depending on local practice, but the principle is complete equality.

Key Fact

The two most important features in the gurdwara prayer hall are the palki (throne-canopy) and the takht (throne or royal seat). Together they represent the sovereignty and living authority of the Guru Granth Sahib.

The Palki and the Takht

The palki is the ornate canopy or palanquin structure under which the Guru Granth Sahib rests. It is typically elaborately decorated and elevated, signalling the supreme honour in which the scripture is held. The palki symbolises the royal status of the Guru Granth Sahib — just as an earthly king might sit under a canopy, the eternal Guru sits under its palki.

The takht (throne) is the raised platform or seat on which the Guru Granth Sahib is placed. The word takht literally means “throne.” Together, the palki (canopy) and the takht (throne) communicate that the Guru Granth Sahib is not just a book — it is the living, reigning Guru of the Sikh community, deserving of the same honour as a Guru in human form. Beside the takht stands the chauri — a fan waved over the Guru Granth Sahib as a mark of honour, similar to the fans once used to cool royalty.

The Guru Granth Sahib is treated with the same care as a living person. At the end of each day in many gurdwaras, the scripture is ceremonially “put to rest” in a dedicated room called the sukhasan room, wrapped in cloth (rumala). In the morning, it is ceremonially brought back to the prayer hall in a procession. This practice underlines the Sikh belief that the Guru Granth Sahib is not a sacred object but a living presence — the Guru who is always available to the community.

The Gurdwara’s Role in the Community

The gurdwara is far more than a place of formal worship. It is the social, cultural and spiritual heart of the Sikh community. The original vision of Guru Nanak was that the gurdwara should serve three interconnected purposes, sometimes described as the three pillars of Sikhism: Naam Japna (meditation on God’s name), Kirat Karni (honest work) and Vand Chakna (sharing with others). All three are expressed in and through the gurdwara.

The gurdwara hosts the langar (free communal kitchen), classes in Punjabi, Sikh history and scripture, ceremonies for birth, naming, marriage and death, and welfare services for those in need. In many British cities, gurdwaras have opened food banks, offered shelter to homeless people, and provided community support during times of national crisis — including during the COVID-19 pandemic. This is sewa in action.

Sikh practice is not confined to the gurdwara. The Guru Granth Sahib at GGS 305:4 emphasises the importance of prayer and remembrance of God in the home. Amritdhari Sikhs observe the Nitnem — a set of daily prayers including Japji Sahib (composed by Guru Nanak) in the morning, and further prayers in the evening and at night. Many Sikh families maintain a dedicated space in the home for the Guru Granth Sahib or for a prayer area. The home is understood as an extension of the gurdwara in spiritual terms — the family that prays together strengthens the sangat in miniature.

Sahajdhari Sikhs — those who follow Sikh teachings but have not undergone formal initiation — may practise Nitnem and maintain home prayer spaces without being bound by all the obligations of the Khalsa. The principle of prayer in the home (GGS 305:4) applies to all Sikhs, amritdhari and sahajdhari alike.

Key Fact

The gurdwara serves the whole community, not just practising Sikhs. It hosts the langar (free communal meal), welfare services, education and ceremonies — expressing the Sikh teaching that sewa (service) is not optional but a dimension of worship. In Britain, gurdwaras have been at the forefront of community support in times of hardship.

title: Amrit Sanskar, the Khalsa and the Five Ks
content_html:
The Khalsa: A Committed Community

On Vaisakhi in 1699, Guru Gobind Singh gathered thousands of Sikhs at Anandpur Sahib. He called for five volunteers willing to sacrifice their lives for their faith. One by one, five men — drawn from five different castes and regions of India — stepped forward. Guru Gobind Singh initiated them into a new community called the Khalsa, meaning “pure” or “belonging to God.” These five — the Panj Pyare (Five Beloved Ones) — became the first members of the Khalsa and remain a model of commitment and equality for Sikhs today.

It is important to understand that not all Sikhs are members of the Khalsa. There are two broad groups in Sikhism: amritdhari Sikhs (those who have been formally initiated) and sahajdhari Sikhs (literally “slow adopters” — those who follow Sikh teaching but have not yet been initiated). Both are accepted within the broader Sikh community, though amritdhari Sikhs have made an additional formal commitment.

Amrit Sanskar: The Initiation Ceremony

Amrit Sanskar (also called “taking amrit” or the baptism of the sword) is the ceremony by which a Sikh is initiated into the Khalsa. The word amrit means “nectar of immortality.” The ceremony is conducted by five amritdhari Sikhs who represent the Panj Pyare. It takes place in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib.

During the ceremony, the Panj Pyare prepare the amrit — a mixture of water and sugar crystals (patasas) — in a steel bowl (bata) while stirring it with a double-edged sword (khanda) and reciting hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib. The candidate kneels before them and receives the amrit in their cupped right hand, which they drink. Amrit is also placed in the eyes and sprinkled over the hair. The ceremony is typically performed at dawn, and the candidate may undergo the ceremony alone or as part of a group.

After taking amrit, the initiate receives the five Ks (Panj Kakars), takes the name Singh (if male) or Kaur (if female), and commits to the Rehat Maryada (the Sikh code of conduct). The ceremony is open to any Sikh who is ready to make this commitment, regardless of caste, gender, nationality or social background — again expressing the Khalsa’s founding principle of equality.

Key Fact

The five Ks (Panj Kakars) are: Kesh (uncut hair), Kangha (wooden comb), Kara (steel bracelet), Kachera (cotton undergarment) and Kirpan (ceremonial sword). They are worn by amritdhari Sikhs as a visible commitment to the Khalsa and to Sikh values.

The Five Ks (Panj Kakars)

Kesh (uncut hair) is the most visible of the five Ks and carries deep meaning. It represents acceptance of God’s creation as it is — the body is not something to be altered but honoured as God-given. Kesh also gave rise to the tradition of the turban (dastar), which amritdhari Sikh men (and some women) wear to keep the uncut hair tidy. The turban is a visible marker of Sikh identity and a source of pride — though it is important to note that the five Ks are obligations on amritdhari Sikhs only, not on all Sikhs. A sahajdhari Sikh does not wear the turban or keep uncut hair as a religious requirement.

Kangha (a small wooden comb) is kept in the hair and symbolises spiritual discipline and order. As the hair is kept tidy and clean, so the mind should be kept ordered and focused on God. Kangha is a reminder that spiritual life requires active maintenance, not passive acceptance.

Kara (a steel bracelet worn on the right wrist) is the most widely worn of the five Ks — even many sahajdhari and non-Khalsa Sikhs choose to wear it. Kara symbolises the unity of God (a circle with no beginning or end), the strength and continuity of the Khalsa community, and a reminder to use one’s hands in God’s service rather than in harm. Its steel also connects to the Khalsa’s warrior tradition.

Kachera (cotton undergarment, a type of shorts) represents self-control and moral restraint — particularly the virtue of brahmcharya (chastity and fidelity in one’s relationships). Kachera also has a practical dimension: it is practical and unrestrictive, symbolising readiness for action in service of the community.

Kirpan (a ceremonial curved sword or dagger) is perhaps the most frequently misunderstood of the five Ks. Kirpan symbolises the duty to defend the weak and stand for justice — not aggression or violence. It reflects the Khalsa’s commitment to sant-sipahi: the “saint-soldier” ideal, combining spiritual devotion (sant) with the courage to defend others (sipahi). The kirpan may vary in size and is typically worn under the clothing. In the UK, the right to carry a kirpan is legally protected as a religious practice for initiated Sikhs.

The five Ks are obligations on amritdhari (initiated) Sikhs. They are not required of sahajdhari Sikhs, who may follow Sikh teaching, pray, attend the gurdwara and practise sewa without having undergone Amrit Sanskar. Some sahajdhari Sikhs choose to wear the kara (steel bracelet) as a personal expression of faith, but this is voluntary. A common misconception is that all Sikhs must wear the kirpan or keep uncut hair. This is not accurate: the five Ks are Khalsa commitments, not universal Sikh requirements. The mark scheme rewards students who distinguish amritdhari and sahajdhari perspectives.

When Guru Gobind Singh initiated the Panj Pyare, he gave all Sikh men the name Singh (meaning “lion”) and all Sikh women the name Kaur (meaning “princess”). This replaced caste-indicating surnames, which in South Asian society had long signalled a person’s social standing. By giving everyone the same name, Guru Gobind Singh enacted the Sikh belief in the equality of all — a Sikh’s identity is defined by their commitment to the Guru and the Khalsa, not by the family they were born into. Many Sikhs today — both amritdhari and sahajdhari — use Singh and Kaur as middle or last names.

Key Fact

The five Ks are obligations on amritdhari (initiated) Sikhs only. Sahajdhari Sikhs follow Sikh teaching without having undergone Amrit Sanskar and are not required to observe the five Ks, though many choose to wear the kara (steel bracelet) as a personal expression of faith.

title: The Oneness of Humanity and Equality
content_html:
One God, One Humanity

The Sikh belief in the oneness of humanity flows directly from Ik Onkar — the oneness of God. Because there is one God, and because God’s light (jot) is present in every human being regardless of caste, religion, gender or nationality, all people are of equal worth and dignity. This is not merely a social ideal in Sikh teaching; it is a theological truth.

When Guru Nanak emerged from the River Bein after three days in what Sikhs believe was a direct encounter with God, his first words were: “There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.” This declaration was radical in its context. Sixteenth-century Punjab was a society stratified by caste, religious division and gender inequality. Guru Nanak proclaimed that God sees none of these divisions; all are equally the creation of the one God.

Key Fact

Guru Nanak’s declaration “There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim” was a foundational statement of the equality of all people before God. He expressed this in practice by sitting and eating with people of all castes — a radical act in a deeply stratified society.

Equality in the Lives of the Gurus

The ten human Gurus embodied the principle of equality throughout their lives. Guru Nanak travelled widely across South Asia and beyond, sharing his message of the oneness of God and humanity with people of all backgrounds. He rejected the caste system and ate and conversed with those considered “untouchable” in the social hierarchy of his day. The institution of langar (the free communal meal, discussed in the Practices unit) was one of his most concrete expressions of equality: all who came to eat sat together on the ground, sharing the same food, regardless of rank or religion.

Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, took the expression of equality a decisive step further when he founded the Khalsa in 1699 at Vaisakhi. He called five people from different castes to step forward and offer their lives for their faith — the Panj Pyare (Five Beloved Ones). By choosing men from different castes and initiating them as equals, Guru Gobind Singh abolished caste hierarchy within the Khalsa. He also gave Sikh men the common name Singh (lion) and Sikh women the name Kaur (princess) — replacing caste-marking surnames with shared names of honour.

Complete Equality of Women

The equality of women with men is stated explicitly in the Guru Granth Sahib and was a central teaching of Guru Nanak. This is highly significant because it was proclaimed in a society in which women had very limited status. The Guru Granth Sahib asks why anyone should consider women inferior when it is women who give birth to the leaders, kings and prophets of the world.

In Sikh practice, this equality has concrete expressions. Women lead worship in the gurdwara, read from the Guru Granth Sahib (granthi), and take part in all aspects of religious life. There is no principle within Sikh teaching that restricts women from any religious role. Amritdhari (initiated) women receive the same initiation as men at Amrit Sanskar, take the name Kaur, and observe the five Ks.

In contemporary British Sikhism, women serve as granthis, sing kirtan (devotional hymns) and organise langar at gurdwaras such as the Gurdwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha in Southall. The principle of equality is woven into everyday Sikh life, not just into theological statements.

Sikh teaching is unambiguous: the caste system is rejected. The Guru Granth Sahib teaches that caste distinctions have no value before God. However, sociological research including studies by the Sikh Network UK has documented that some Sikh communities in Britain continue to observe informal caste distinctions in social and marriage practices. This is a tension between stated religious teaching and lived practice. For the purposes of the exam, students should note: the teaching of Sikhism is complete equality, including abolition of caste. Where practice diverges from teaching, this is seen by many Sikhs as a deviation from authentic Sikh values, not as a sanctioned tradition.

Equality in the Guru Granth Sahib

The equality of all people is encoded in the Guru Granth Sahib in a remarkable way. The scripture contains the writings not only of the Sikh Gurus but also of Muslim, Hindu and other composers from different castes and backgrounds — among them Kabir (a low-caste weaver), Sheikh Farid (a Muslim mystic) and Ravidas (a leatherworker considered among the lowest in caste hierarchy). By including their hymns alongside those of the Gurus, the Guru Granth Sahib enacts the teaching it proclaims: all who seek God are equally worthy.

At the Gurdwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha in Southall — the largest gurdwara in Europe — the langar serves thousands of people every week, with no charge and no distinction of religion, class or background. Visitors of all faiths are welcome. This practice directly enacts the Sikh teaching of the oneness of humanity. The Network of Sikh Organisations (NSO) actively promotes Sikh values of equality and interfaith dialogue in British civic life, demonstrating that equality is a living commitment, not just a historical teaching.

Key Fact

Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa in 1699, choosing the first five members (Panj Pyare) from different castes. He gave all Sikh men the name Singh and all Sikh women the name Kaur — replacing caste-marking surnames to express that, before God, all Sikhs are equally lion-hearted and equally honoured.

title: The Nature of God and the Mool Mantra
content_html:
Sikhism: A Living Tradition

Sikhism is one of the world’s youngest major religions, founded by Guru Nanak in the Punjab region of South Asia in the late fifteenth century. It is important to understand from the outset that Sikhism is a distinct, independent religion — not a synthesis of Hinduism and Islam, even though it emerged in a region where both traditions were present. Guru Nanak received what Sikhs believe was a direct revelation from God, and the teachings he proclaimed stand on their own foundations. Today there are approximately 430,000 Sikhs living in Britain, with large communities in Southall (west London), Birmingham, Leicester and Bradford.

The Mool Mantra: The Foundation of Sikh Belief

At the very opening of the Guru Granth Sahib (GGS 1a) stands the Mool Mantra (also spelled Mul Mantar). The phrase “Mool Mantra” means “root formula” or “foundational verse.” It is the first composition in the Guru Granth Sahib and is considered by Sikhs to be the most complete summary of their belief in God. The Mool Mantra opens with the numeral 1 — in Punjabi script, Ik Onkar — followed by a series of attributes.

The Mool Mantra teaches that God is: one (Ik Onkar); the Truth (Sat Nam — whose name is truth); the Creator (Karta Purakh); without fear (Nirbhau); without enmity (Nirvair); beyond time and death (Akal Murat); self-existent (Ajooni Saibhang); and known through the grace of the Guru (Gur Prasad). These attributes paint a picture of God as both utterly transcendent — beyond human comprehension — and intimately present within creation.

Key Fact

The Mool Mantra (GGS 1a) opens with Ik Onkar — “There is one God.” This single statement of absolute monotheism is the cornerstone of all Sikh belief. It is displayed in gurdwaras across Britain and is often the first Punjabi phrase a Sikh child learns.

God as Creator

Sikh teaching holds that God is Karta Purakh — the “Doer,” the Creator being. The universe exists because of God’s hukam (divine will or command). This concept of God as Creator has two dimensions that students must be able to distinguish: God shown in and through the universe, and God as separate from the universe.

First, Sikh teaching holds that God’s presence is visible within creation. The natural world — its beauty, its order, its interdependence — reflects and reveals the divine. Looking at a sunrise over the River Beas near Amritsar, or the community gathered at the Golden Temple, a Sikh sees not just the physical world but a manifestation of divine glory. In this sense God is immanent — permeating all things.

Second, Sikh teaching is clear that God is not identical to the created world. God existed before creation and will exist after it ends. God is not limited by time or physical form. In this sense God is transcendent — entirely other than and beyond the universe. The Mool Mantra’s phrase Akal Murat (deathless form) captures this: God is beyond the cycle of birth, death and decay that governs all created things.

Some students assume that a God who is transcendent (beyond creation) cannot also be immanent (present within creation). Sikh teaching holds both simultaneously. God’s light (jot) is present in every living being, so in that sense God is intimately close. Yet God is also beyond all names, forms and descriptions. The Guru Granth Sahib describes God as nirguna (without attributes — beyond description) and saguna (with attributes — known through creation and the Gurus). This dual nature is not a contradiction for Sikhs; it reflects the vastness of the divine that cannot be confined to any single description.

This matters for the exam. A common student error is to write that “Sikhs believe God IS the universe” (pantheism) or that “God is completely separate and distant.” Neither is accurate. Sikh teaching is that God is present throughout creation (immanent) AND separate from and greater than creation (transcendent).

Ik Onkar and Strict Monotheism

The numeral “1” at the start of the Mool Mantra is not accidental. Guru Nanak’s first public declaration, recorded in the Janamsakhis, was “Na koi Hindu, na koi Musalman” — “There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.” This was a proclamation that divisions of religion, caste and status do not exist before God. The oneness of God (Ik Onkar) leads directly to the oneness of humanity. Because there is one God, all people share the same divine light within them.

Sikh monotheism is strict. There are no lesser gods or goddesses, no trinity of divine persons, and no deity who is God’s equal or rival. God is addressed in the Guru Granth Sahib by many names — Waheguru (Wondrous Lord), Hari, Ram, Allah — but these are understood as different names for the one, same God. The use of diverse names reflects Guru Nanak’s vision that all humanity, of different faiths and backgrounds, is reaching for the same ultimate reality.

Waheguru is the name most commonly used by Sikhs when speaking of or addressing God. Literally meaning “Wondrous Lord” or “Wonderful Guru,” it captures the sense of awe at God’s greatness. At the Gurdwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha in Southall — the largest gurdwara in Europe — the congregational greeting is Waheguru Ji Ka Khalsa, Waheguru Ji Ki Fateh (“The Khalsa belongs to the Wondrous Lord; victory belongs to the Wondrous Lord”). This salutation embodies Sikh belief that all belongs to God.

Key Fact

The Mool Mantra describes God as Nirbhau (without fear) and Nirvair (without enmity). These two attributes are linked: because God has no enemies and no fears, God’s love for all creation is completely unconditional. This underpins the Sikh teaching of equality — God’s love is not withheld from any person on the grounds of caste, gender or religion.
